fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Backlash From Asking Questions", "body": "Chance opens by saying that two episodes questioning the Tartaria old world reset theory drew more hostility than anything else he has published in roughly a decade of podcasting, more even than flat Earth pushback or refusing to mask during the pandemic. He describes being accused of Freemasonry, of shilling for the mainstream historical record, and of secretly working for the Smithsonian. He is careful to say most listeners are not like this, but argues that a subset behaves in a cult adjacent way, since holding the belief requires dismissing evidence placed directly in front of you."}, {"title": "Primary Sources Over YouTube Videos", "body": "The turn started when a Patreon supporter sent Chance an archive of more than 700 construction photographs from the 1893 Chicago World's Fair. He admits that before that he had only watched videos and interviewed people who made videos, which he had mistaken for research. Now he uses AI assisted search to reach digitized archives Google cannot surface, then combs the records himself, spending hours hunting nineteenth century newspapers. He draws a hard line between a history book, which he calls a secondary source, and a primary source, meaning the physical document sitting in a state archive box."}, {"title": "The Genre Template And The Motte", "body": "Chance says he mapped the recurring formula in Tartaria content: an incredulous tone, plus four or five stock lines such as no records or blueprints exist, they lacked the technology, they built it with suppressed technology, everyone died at thirty, the photos are fake, this old map proves it. He notes the claims often contradict each other within one video. He then walks through the Motte and Bailey fallacy, named for medieval castle design, where a creator advances an outrageous claim, retreats under challenge to the safe position that history is written by victors, then later behaves as though the outrageous claim held."}, {"title": "The Asylum Files, Receipts And All", "body": "The longest evidence stretch concerns nineteenth century insane asylums. Answering a YouTuber's claim that a coordinated national effort is suspicious, Chance points to Franklin Pierce vetoing a bill on May 3, 1854 that would have handed states ten million acres to fund care for the indigent insane, which means funding was state by state. He cites Missouri legislative appendices, an architect's bid of $47,450 that ran past $50,000, an Iowa appropriation of $125,000 plus 320 donated acres, a Buchanan County newspaper donor list, and architect Stephen Von Shipman, whom the video claimed could not be found."}, {"title": "What Chance Still Grants The Theorists", "body": "He does not dismiss everything. He agrees the fairs carried genuine propaganda, with elites seeding an American mythology, and says mainstream historians accept that too. He found that Chicago deliberately raised its street grade, partially burying existing buildings, and grants that liquefaction during earthquakes is real, so he has not closed the mud flood question. He credits the era's craftsmanship, blaming the later decline on central banking and fiat currency rather than a lost civilization. On Maple Leaf Gardens, built June to November 1931, he cites 1,200 workers on three shifts, stock paid as wages, and 1884 and 1910 Toronto maps showing housing."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Is the Tartarian Empire and “Old World” reset theory hiding a forgotten chapter of history, or has conspiracy culture created a mythology of its own? The goal isn’t to defend mainstream history. It’s to ask a harder question: what can we actually demonstrate from the surviving evidence? But the deeper subject may be the psychology of conspiracy culture itself: incredulity as a content formula, unfalsifiable claims, shifting standards of evidence, the Motte-and-Bailey fallacy, algorithmic incentives, and the emergence of alternative orthodoxies inside communities originally built around questioning authority.
